Une molécule est polaire si les charges: A molecule is polar if its charges are unevenly distributed: water is, hence its properties as a solvent.
Les liaisons hydrogène entre molécules d: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules explain its high boiling point.
La glace flotte parce que ses liaisons h: Ice floats because its hydrogen bonds arrange it in a more open lattice than liquid water.
pH < 7 : acide ; pH = 7 : neutre ; pH >: pH < 7: acidic; pH = 7: neutral; pH > 7: basic.

Équations, combustion, catalyse, oxydati: Equations, combustion, catalysis, oxidation and reduction.
Une équation chimique doit être équilibr: A chemical equation must be balanced: the same number of atoms of each kind on both sides (Lavoisier).
Combustion : un combustible + du dioxygè: Combustion: a fuel + oxygen → CO₂, water and heat.
Un catalyseur accélère une réaction sans: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being consumed. Oxidation: loss of electrons; reduction: gain.
La rouille n'est pas une simple « saleté: Rust is not just “dirt”: it is oxidized iron, bulkier, which cracks the metal.
Une équation équilibrée : 4 H et 2 O de: A balanced equation: 4 H and 2 O on each side
Solide, liquide, gaz, changements d'état: Solid, liquid, gas, changes of state and the gas laws.
Solide, liquide, gaz : même matière, agi: Solid, liquid, gas: the same matter, with different agitation and distance between molecules.
Fusion, vaporisation, condensation, soli: Melting, vaporization, condensation, solidification, sublimation (solid → gas), deposition (gas → solid).

À volume fixé, la pression d'un gaz augm: At fixed volume, the pressure of a gas rises with temperature (PV = nRT).
L'eau bout à moins de 100 °C en altitude: Water boils below 100 °C at altitude: about 70 °C at the top of Everest.
Le carbone, les hydrocarbures, les polym: Carbon, hydrocarbons, polymers and the molecules of life.
La chimie organique est celle des compos: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds; carbon forms four bonds.
Hydrocarbures : uniquement carbone et hy: Hydrocarbons: only carbon and hydrogen (methane, butane, octane).
Polymères : longues chaînes d'unités rép: Polymers: long chains of repeating units (polyethylene, DNA, cellulose).
Les glucides, lipides, protéines et acid: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids are the great molecules of life.
« Chimique » ne s'oppose pas à « naturel: “Chemical” is not the opposite of “natural”: everything alive is made of organic molecules.
Un polymère : une chaîne de petites unit: A polymer: a chain of small units
Cuisine, savon, médicaments, piles et ma: Cooking, soap, medicines, batteries and materials.

La réaction de Maillard (sucres + protéi: The Maillard reaction (sugars + proteins with heat) browns bread and sears meat.
Une pile transforme une réaction d'oxydo: A battery turns a redox reaction into a current.
Le paracétamol et l'aspirine sont des mo: Paracetamol and aspirin are synthetic molecules; aspirin derives from willow bark.
Mélanger eau de Javel et vinaigre dégage: Mixing bleach and vinegar releases toxic chlorine: never combine household products.
Isotopes, demi-vie, fission, fusion et d: Isotopes, half-life, fission, fusion and dating.
Demi-vie : le temps pour que la moitié d: Half-life: the time for half of the radioactive nuclei to decay. It does not depend on the quantity.
Le carbone 14 (demi-vie ≈ 5 730 ans) dat: Carbon-14 (half-life ≈ 5,730 years) dates organic remains up to about 50,000 years.
Fission : un noyau lourd se casse (centr: Fission: a heavy nucleus splits (power plants). Fusion: light nuclei join (the Sun).
α arrêté par une feuille de papier, β pa: α is stopped by a sheet of paper, β by a few millimeters of aluminum, γ by lead or thick concrete.
Après deux demi-vies, il ne reste pas zé: After two half-lives, what remains is not zero but a quarter.
pH = −log[H⁺] : 10⁻³ mol/L d'ions H⁺ don: pH = −log[H⁺]: 10⁻³ mol/L of H⁺ ions gives a pH of 3, 10⁻⁷ gives 7.
Une mole de gaz parfait à 0 °C sous une: One mole of ideal gas at 0 °C and one atmosphere takes up about 22.4 L.
Un noyau minuscule dans beaucoup de vide: A tiny nucleus in a lot of emptiness
Protons et neutrons dans le noyau, élect: Protons and neutrons in the nucleus, electrons around it. The nucleus carries almost all the mass, but the atom is mostly empty space (Rutherford, 1911).
Un atome, c'est un noyau, fait de proton: An atom is a nucleus, made of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons. Almost all of its mass is in the nucleus, and yet the nucleus is tiny: the atom is 27,000 to 60,000 times wider, depending on the element. If the nucleus were a marble, the atom would be the size of a stadium.
On l'a compris en tirant dessus. Entre 1: We found out by shooting at it. Between 1906 and 1913, in Manchester, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at a very thin gold foil, under Ernest Rutherford's direction. Almost all went straight through, but a few bounced back. In 1911 Rutherford drew the conclusion: the positive charge and the mass are packed into a very small centre, the nucleus.
Le numéro qui fait l'élément: The number that makes the element
Protons = identité de l'élément. Neutron: Protons = the element's identity. More or fewer neutrons = isotope. More or fewer electrons = ion.
Les neutrons, eux, peuvent varier sans c: Neutrons can vary without changing the element: that gives isotopes. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons; the second has two more neutrons. Electrons can vary too: an atom that gains or loses some becomes a charged ion, like Na⁺ or Cl⁻ in salt.
Une colonne du tableau = une famille aux: A column of the table = a family with similar properties. Mendeleev (1869) predicted missing elements, found later: gallium, scandium, germanium.
En 1869, Dmitri Mendeleïev range les élé: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the known elements in a table: in rows by increasing mass, and in columns grouping elements with similar chemical properties. Where nothing fitted, he left empty boxes and announced that unknown elements would fill them.
Il les nomme d'avance : eka-aluminium, e: He named them in advance: eka-aluminium, eka-boron, eka-silicon. Gallium was discovered in 1875 by Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, scandium in 1879, germanium in 1886: they took the predicted places. That is what made his table prevail.
Liaison covalente = une paire d'électron: Covalent bond = a shared pair of electrons (Lewis, 1916). Single, double or triple depending on the number of pairs. Carbon makes 4 bonds.
En 1916, Gilbert Lewis propose une idée: In 1916 Gilbert Lewis proposed a simple idea: two atoms stay bonded when they share a pair of electrons. That is the covalent bond. In H₂, each hydrogen brings one electron; the pair belongs to both at once.
Deux atomes peuvent partager une, deux o: Two atoms can share one, two or three pairs: a single, double or triple bond. The two oxygens of O₂ are joined by a double bond. Carbon, with its four valence electrons, forms four bonds: that is what lets it build chains and rings.
Électronégativité (Pauling, 1932) : peti: Electronegativity (Pauling, 1932): small gap = covalent, medium gap = polar, large gap (over 1.7) = ionic.
Dans une liaison, les deux atomes ne tir: In a bond, the two atoms do not pull on the electrons with the same strength. Linus Pauling put a number on it in 1932: electronegativity. Fluorine is the greediest (3.98), oxygen follows (3.44), hydrogen is at 2.20, sodium at 0.93.
Tout dépend de l'écart. Presque nul (jus: It all depends on the gap. Almost none (up to about 0.3): fair sharing. Between 0.3 and 1.7: the bond is polar, one side carries a little negative charge. Above 1.7 it is usually ionic: one atom simply takes the electron. Between sodium and chlorine (3.16) the gap is over 2: salt is made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. These thresholds are guides, not sharp borders.
L'eau est polaire et coudée ; ses liaiso: Water is polar and bent; its hydrogen bonds explain its boiling at 100 °C and floating ice.
Ces accroches expliquent les bizarreries: These grips explain water's oddities. Hydrogen sulfide, H₂S, almost twice as heavy, is a gas at room temperature, while water only boils at 100 °C. And on freezing, hydrogen bonds arrange the molecules in an open lattice: ice (0.917 g/mL) is about 9 % less dense than liquid water. It floats, and lakes freeze from the top.
Une échelle qui compte par dix: A scale that counts in tens
pH = −log[H⁺] (Sørensen, 1909). Une unit: pH = −log[H⁺] (Sørensen, 1909). One unit lower = 10 times more acidic.
En 1909, au laboratoire Carlsberg de Cop: In 1909, at the Carlsberg laboratory in Copenhagen, Søren Sørensen invented pH to measure acidity. Below 7 a solution is acidic; at 7, neutral; above, basic. Lemon juice is around 2, vinegar around 3, pure water 7, bleach around 12.
Le piège, c'est que l'échelle est logari: The catch is that the scale is logarithmic: pH is the exponent of the H⁺ ion concentration, with its sign changed. 10⁻³ mol/L gives a pH of 3, 10⁻⁴ a pH of 4. Going down by a single unit therefore means ten times more H⁺ ions; by two units, a hundred times more.
Un acide donne, une base prend: An acid gives, a base takes
Acide = donneur de H⁺, base = capteur de: Acid = H⁺ donor, base = H⁺ acceptor (Brønsted and Lowry, 1923). Acid + base → salt + water.
La définition la plus utile date de 1923: The most useful definition dates from 1923: the Dane Johannes Brønsted and the Englishman Martin Lowry, independently, said an acid is a species that gives up an H⁺ ion, and a base one that takes it. Before them, Svante Arrhenius, building on his 1884 work on ions in water, spoke of acids that release H⁺ in solution.
Quand un acide rencontre une base en bon: When an acid meets a base in the right proportions, the H⁺ of one and the OH⁻ of the other form water, and a salt remains: that is neutralisation. That is what the bicarbonate in a heartburn remedy does: it neutralises part of the hydrochloric acid in gastric juice.
Le sang ne plaisante pas avec le pH: Blood does not joke about pH
Un tampon (acide faible + sa base) amort: A buffer (weak acid + its base) dampens pH changes: blood stays between 7.35 and 7.45 thanks to bicarbonate.
Le sang humain se tient entre pH 7,35 et: Human blood stays between pH 7.35 and 7.45. Outside that narrow window, acidosis or alkalosis sets in quickly. What holds it there is a buffer: a weak acid and base pair, here carbonic acid and bicarbonate, which soaks up extra H⁺ or supplies it when it runs short.
Les océans, eux, n'ont pas un tampon inf: The oceans do not have an infinite buffer. They absorb part of the CO₂ we emit, which forms carbonic acid: surface pH has gone from about 8.2 to 8.1 since the 19th century. Only a tenth of a unit, but on a scale that counts in tens, that is about 30 % more H⁺ ions.
Rien ne se crée : on recompte les atomes: Nothing is created: count the atoms again
Conservation de la masse (Lomonossov 175: Conservation of mass (Lomonosov 1756, Lavoisier 1773): as many atoms of each kind before and after.
Un bois qui brûle semble perdre du poids: Burning wood seems to lose weight, rusting metal seems to gain some. Antoine Lavoisier ran reactions in sealed vessels and weighed everything: the total mass does not change. He stated it as early as 1773 and popularised the principle, which buried the phlogiston theory. The Russian Mikhail Lomonosov had stated it as early as 1756.
Dans une réaction, les atomes changent d: In a reaction, atoms change partners; they are neither born nor destroyed. Hence balancing: in 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, there are 4 hydrogens and 2 oxygens on each side. If the counts do not match, the equation is wrong.
Énergie d'activation (Arrhenius, 1889) :: Activation energy (Arrhenius, 1889): the barrier to get over. Heat = more molecules get over; catalyst = lower barrier, without being used up.
Une allumette ne s'enflamme pas toute se: A match does not light by itself in its box: it has to be struck. Every reaction has an energy barrier to get over, the activation energy, a term introduced by Svante Arrhenius in 1889. The hotter it is, the more molecules have enough energy to get over: that is why the fridge slows the reactions that spoil food.
Un catalyseur abaisse cette barrière : l: A catalyst lowers that barrier: the reaction goes faster, and the catalyst comes out unchanged. It changes neither the starting point nor the end point, only the path. Enzymes are life's catalysts; a car's catalytic converter is another.
Oxydation = perte d'électrons, réduction: Oxidation = loss of electrons, reduction = gain. A battery sends those electrons through a circuit (Volta, 1800).
S'oxyder, c'est perdre des électrons ; s: To be oxidised is to lose electrons; to be reduced is to gain them. The two always go together: the electrons lost by one are taken by the other. Rusting iron is oxidised; the oxygen attacking it is reduced.
Si l'on force ces électrons à passer par: If those electrons are forced through a wire, you get a current. That was Alessandro Volta's idea; he described his pile to the Royal Society on 20 March 1800: stacked zinc and copper discs, separated by cloth soaked in brine. All our batteries still work that way.
Solide, liquide, gaz = mêmes molécules,: Solid, liquid, gas = same molecules, different jiggling. Sublimation = solid → gas directly.
Glace, eau, vapeur : ce sont les mêmes m: Ice, water, steam: the same H₂O molecules. What changes is how much they jiggle and how far apart they are. In a solid they vibrate in place; in a liquid they slide past each other; in a gas they fly off and spread out.
Pourquoi le glaçon reste à 0 °C: Why the ice cube stays at 0 °C
Pendant un changement d'état, la tempéra: During a change of state, the temperature stays constant. Melting 1 g of ice ≈ heating 1 g of water by 80 °C.
C'est pour cela que la glace refroidit s: That is why ice cools a drink so well: it soaks up heat without warming up. And salt on an icy road heats nothing: it lowers the temperature at which water freezes, down to about −21 °C for salt water.
P × V constant à température fixe (Boyle: P × V constant at fixed temperature (Boyle 1662, Mariotte 1676); P V = n R T (Clapeyron, 1834). Lower pressure = lower boiling point.
À température constante, si on divise pa: At constant temperature, halve a gas's volume and its pressure doubles: P × V stays constant. Robert Boyle published it in 1662, Edme Mariotte in 1676. Émile Clapeyron combined these laws in 1834 into a single formula, P V = n R T: pressure, volume, amount of gas and temperature are linked.
Une conséquence concrète : la températur: A concrete consequence: the boiling point depends on pressure. Under one atmosphere water boils at 100 °C; at altitude the air weighs less and it boils earlier, around 70 °C at the top of Everest. Pasta cooks badly there, and the opposite happens in a pressure cooker, where pressure rises and water goes above 100 °C.
Organique = chimie du carbone, qui fait: Organic = carbon chemistry; carbon makes 4 bonds. Wöhler (1828) synthesised urea, but did not kill vitalism on his own.
La chimie organique, c'est la chimie des: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. With its four bonds, carbon links to itself in chains, branches and rings, and to hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen: hence millions of different molecules, from methane CH₄ to proteins.
On a longtemps cru qu'il fallait une « f: People long believed a "vital force" was needed to make these molecules. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler obtained urea from mineral compounds. Textbooks often make it the death blow to vitalism, but that is a simplified legend: Wöhler was not on a crusade, and other syntheses, such as Kolbe's acetic acid in 1845, counted just as much.
Benzène : isolé par Faraday (1825), anne: Benzene: isolated by Faraday (1825), 6-carbon ring proposed by Kekulé (1865). The snake dream was told in 1890.
Le benzène, isolé par Michael Faraday en: Benzene, isolated by Michael Faraday in 1825, was long a puzzle: six carbons, six hydrogens, and yet surprisingly stable. In 1865 August Kekulé proposed a ring of six carbons, with alternating single and double bonds.
En 1890, pour les 25 ans de sa découvert: In 1890, for the 25th anniversary of his discovery, Kekulé told how the idea came to him while daydreaming by the fire: a snake biting its own tail. A nice story, told a quarter of a century later; nobody knows how far to believe it. The ring stayed: it is found in aspirin, paracetamol and polystyrene.
Polymère = longue chaîne d'un motif répé: Polymer = long chain of a repeated unit (plastics, cellulose, DNA). Staudinger (1920, Nobel 1953) made the case against general opinion.
Un polymère est une molécule immense fai: A polymer is a huge molecule made of a unit repeated thousands of times. The polyethylene of bags is a chain of –CH₂–CH₂–. Nature is full of them: wood's cellulose, starch, proteins, DNA.
En 1920, Hermann Staudinger affirme que: In 1920 Hermann Staudinger claimed that rubber or cellulose were real long chains held by covalent bonds. The big names of the day, such as Emil Fischer, did not believe it: to them these were clumps of small molecules. Staudinger held firm and received the Nobel Prize in 1953. Meanwhile Bakelite (1907) and nylon (1935) had launched the plastic age.
Savon = graisse + soude (saponification): Soap = fat + lye (saponification). A head that likes water, a tail that likes grease: micelles carry the dirt away.
Le savon se fabrique en mélangeant des g: Soap is made by mixing fats or oils with a strong base, lye: the fats split into fatty acid salts, and glycerol is left over. That is saponification. Traces of soap-like materials go back to about 2800 BCE, in Babylon.
Chaque molécule de savon a une tête qui: Each soap molecule has a head that likes water and a tail that likes grease. In water the tails dive into the grease while the heads stay on the outside: they form little balls, micelles, that trap the dirt. Rinsing carries them away.
Maillard (1912) : sucres + acides aminés: Maillard (1912): sugars + amino acids + heat (140 to 165 °C) = browning and aromas. No crust in boiling water.
La croûte du pain, la viande grillée, le: Bread crust, grilled meat, roasted coffee: that is the Maillard reaction, described in 1912 by the French chemist Louis Camille Maillard. Sugars and amino acids react with heat and produce hundreds of brown, fragrant molecules.
Elle va vite autour de 140 à 165 °C. Voi: It goes fast at around 140 to 165 °C. That is why boiled meat does not brown: in water you cannot go above 100 °C. To sear, you need a hot pan and a dry surface.
Du saule à l'aspirine, et ce qu'il ne fa: From willow to aspirin, and what not to mix
Aspirin comes from willow (Bayer, 1899). Bleach + acid = toxic chlorine: never mix household products.
Les plantes riches en salicylés, comme l: Salicylate-rich plants such as willow already appear on Sumerian tablets and in the Egyptian Ebers papyrus; around 400 BCE Hippocrates described a tea against fever. In 1897, at Bayer, chemists looked for a version gentler on the stomach, and by 1899 acetylsalicylic acid was sold worldwide under the name Aspirin.
La chimie de la maison a aussi ses dange: Household chemistry has its dangers too. Bleach mixed with an acid, such as a descaler or vinegar, releases chlorine gas, which is toxic. Simple rule: never mix two household products.
Une plaque voilée dans un tiroir: A fogged plate in a drawer
Becquerel (1896), les Curie (1898). Alph: Becquerel (1896), the Curies (1898). Alpha: paper; beta: aluminium; gamma: lead or concrete.
En 1896, Henri Becquerel range des sels: In 1896 Henri Becquerel put uranium salts on a photographic plate in a drawer, for lack of sunshine for his experiment. The plate was fogged anyway: uranium gives off radiation on its own. In 1898 Marie and Pierre Curie discovered two far more active elements, polonium and radium.
En 1899, Ernest Rutherford trie ces rayo: In 1899 Ernest Rutherford sorted these rays by what stops them: he called alpha those stopped by a few thin sheets, beta those that get through. Gamma came later. Alpha particles, helium nuclei, stop on a sheet of paper; beta on a few millimetres of aluminium; gamma rays, a very energetic light, need lead or thick concrete.
La moitié, puis la moitié de la moitié: Half, then half of the half
Demi-vie : la moitié se désintègre, quel: Half-life: half decays, whatever the amount. Carbon-14: 5,730 years, dating back to about 50,000 years (Libby).
On ne peut pas prévoir quand un noyau ra: Nobody can predict when a radioactive nucleus will decay, but we know how long it takes for half of a batch to do so: the half-life. It does not depend on the amount. After one half-life half remains, after two a quarter, after three an eighth: never zero all at once.
Le carbone 14 en fait une horloge. Il na: Carbon-14 turns this into a clock. It is born high in the atmosphere, when neutrons produced by cosmic rays strike nitrogen. Living things take it in while they live, then the stock runs down with a half-life of about 5,730 years. Willard Libby developed the method in Chicago in the late 1940s (Nobel Prize 1960); it reaches back about 50,000 years.
Fission (Hahn et Strassmann 1938, Meitne: Fission (Hahn and Strassmann 1938, Meitner and Frisch 1939): a heavy nucleus splits, chain reaction (Chicago, 1942). Fusion: light nuclei join (the Sun).
En décembre 1938, Otto Hahn et Fritz Str: In December 1938, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found barium after bombarding uranium with neutrons: the nucleus had split in two. In early 1939 Lise Meitner and her nephew Otto Frisch explained it, and Frisch called it fission, like the division of cells. Each fission releases about 200 MeV and neutrons that can trigger others: a chain reaction.
Le 2 décembre 1942, sous les gradins du: On 2 December 1942, under the stands of Stagg Field at the University of Chicago, on a former squash court, Enrico Fermi's pile, uranium in 45,000 graphite blocks, sustained the first controlled chain reaction, at about half a watt. The Sun does the opposite: it fuses hydrogen nuclei into helium.
Ce qui fait qu'un atome est du carbone p: What makes an atom carbon rather than nitrogen is its number of protons: the atomic number. Carbon has 6, oxygen 8, iron 26. Change that number and you change the element. It was the young English physicist Henry Moseley who showed it in 1913, by measuring the X-rays of the elements: the atomic number is the charge of the nucleus, and it put the table in order. He was killed two years later at Gallipoli, on 10 August 1915, aged 27.
Dans l'eau, l'oxygène tire les électrons: In water, oxygen pulls the electrons harder than the hydrogens, and the molecule is bent, at about 104.5°: a negative side (oxygen) and a positive side (the hydrogens). It is polar. The hydrogen side of one molecule clings to the oxygen side of a neighbour: that is the hydrogen bond, and each molecule can form up to four. That water is not an element but a compound of hydrogen and oxygen was announced by Lavoisier and Laplace to the Academy of Sciences in November 1783. Henry Cavendish had made water by burning hydrogen as early as 1781, without reading it that way.
Chaque passage a son nom : fusion (solid: Each transition has its name: melting (solid → liquid), vaporisation (liquid → gas), condensation (gas → liquid), solidification (liquid → solid), sublimation (solid → gas directly, like dry ice). Heat a gas further and its atoms lose electrons: that is plasma, the stuff of stars and lightning. The word plasma was proposed in 1928 by the American chemist Irving Langmuir.
Pendant qu'un glaçon fond, sa températur: While an ice cube melts, its temperature does not move: 0 °C from start to finish. The energy it receives does not heat it; it takes the crystal apart. And it takes a lot: 334 J to melt one gram of ice, almost as much as to heat that same gram of liquid water from 0 to 80 °C. This hidden heat, latent heat, was first presented by the Scot Joseph Black on 23 April 1762 at the University of Glasgow: ice and water at 0 °C left in the same room, the water warms quickly, the ice stays at 0 °C.
